utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just warn the witness that you are still bound by the declaration you made yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much. Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we started the cross-examination. Today we are going to finish it, Mr. Miljanic. Yesterday you stated that in September 1991, you were appointed commander of the defence in Skabrnja and that under your command in Skabrnja itself there were 242 people, either reserve policemen or volunteers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the moment when on the 2nd of October 1991, women, children and the elderly, in agreement with the Crisis Staff of the municipality, were evacuated by buses temporarily from Skabrnja; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you said that these 242 men stayed behind in the village with the task of protecting the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also said that at that time you were 42 years of age and that you were the oldest person there, or among the oldest people there among the people who remained to protect the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one thing: Who mobilised these 242 men who stayed behind in the village? How did that happen? How come they came to be under your command?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not real mobilisation. I as a soldier know what mobilisation is and what mobilisation call-up is. Quite simply, at that time the chief of the police administration, Mr. Ivan Brzoja, sent reserve policemen who were from Skabrnja. He sent them to go to Skabrnja in order to secure peace and protection for the village. The others were exclusively volunteers, not mobilised people, volunteers only, who made themselves available, who said that they would be in the village and protect the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the average, they were between the age of 30 and 35. I'm referring to the reservists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Were they the only ones who were armed in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps. There were perhaps a few civilians there who came from Zadar to see how their cattle were doing, feed them, et cetera, to see their property. These were hunters and others. Well, I mean others who were not hunters did not have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because in your statement to the district court in Zadar on page 8, you said that some elderly people also had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You mean the hunters who came?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the hunters. Well, every day people came from Zadar because they had horses, cows, sheep, their cattle, their property, and they had feed their animals. They were hunters. In Skabrnja there were about 25 to 30 hunters, most of them older people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, may I remind you please to wait a moment after the question by the counsel so that you don't overlap. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, as a military expert, how would you characterise this group of 243 men?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would characterise them in the following way: Before the war, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, there was a Territorial Defence. I consider them to be the members of the Territorial Defence because at that time we did not have a military establishment, so that is why they had names from the Yugoslav People's Army. So we had squads, platoons, companies. So it was only based on the Territorial Defence principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That group of 240 men could be considered a battalion, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, with the others attached, along with the villages that I mentioned yesterday, in my answers yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In those seven villages you had 730 to 740 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, give or take ten men up and down. People went and came back, but roughly that was the number, that's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We should just pause between questions and answers so that all of this gets interpreted. In your statement to the OTP, you said that in Skabrnja you made two barricades, you put up two barricades, one at the entrance to the village and the other one in the middle of Skabrnja on the road to Biljane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At one of these barricades, your men took two JNA officers prisoner. One was Dean Brener and the other one was a certain Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. Not at the barricade, not at the roadblock, but above the village in the forest, above the houses, in the forest. They did not take the road when they were coming, they came through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But it is correct that these were their names?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and among them Petar Sveljo, a policeman, a third person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Your men brought these officers to you for questioning, right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How did you treat them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very fairly and properly. I repeat: Very fairly and properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How much time did they spend there with you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About two and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Who were they handed over to there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the police came and took them -- well, I don't know what happened later in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was that the military police of the ZNG, the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be sure. I cannot be sure. But I think -- well, quite simply I'm not sure whether they were active policemen or members of the ZNG. I can no longer remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, did the members of your battalion take other prisoners, some members of the JNA, officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, above the village itself, two or three soldiers, I can no longer remember. I know that one was from Varazdin. Two or three. And the other 80 soldiers came on their own to us. They came armed, they handed over their weapons, and they said that they fled from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very fairly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we slow down? The interpreter did not hear the question. I know that when we get heated with the questions, we want to go faster, but can we give it our time, please. Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Thank you, Mr. Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How were these soldiers treated, the ones that you talked about just now?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very fairly, very properly. And they were all sent to Zadar. All of them were sent to Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... 80 that came voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it wasn't in one day. It happened throughout those ten or 15 days. People kept coming. Sometimes it would be five people, sometimes seven, ten, whatever. But at any rate, it was a total of 80 something soldiers. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it is those 80 that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the district court in Zadar, you stated at the time that your men captured over 50 enemy officers and soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said then, that -- there is evidence they came on their own, but I don't know, I wrote it that way because of some court or something, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On the same occasion, before the district court in Zadar, you mentioned a special purpose unit under the command of a certain Djuro Zupan that arrived in Skabrnja. Whose unit was that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a special unit, a platoon of a special unit of the Zadar MUP. The commander was Djuro Zupan. That unit came on the 15th or the 16th, and until the 17th in the morning it was there. On the morning of the 17th it left Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The Prosecutor seems to have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Actually, it's not an objection, I was merely hoping to have a reference, when the statement to the district court in Zadar is mentioned, the date and so on, which statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll provide one straight away. It was given on the 16th of November -- sorry, the 5th of October 1992. And the subjects we were discussing are on page 3. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we able to get a copy, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You don't have English translations?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is a copy of the English translation attached to the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that yet again they have not received the documents from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any copies for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have some copies. These could be passed to the interpreters, if it assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We appreciate your help. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is page 3, paragraph 5, in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. We have seen the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, your battalion from Skabrnja, did it have some joint plan with the unit that was commanded by Djuro Zupan?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It did not have any plan. We just had an attempt to reach an agreement orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In respect of what?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it would be necessary to carry out reconnaissance and to attack tanks that were above me, about a kilometre or two into Veljane.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: This tank group, did it belong to the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Yugoslav People's Army. I have already said that Mr. Brener had informed me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: However, you have not carried out that task -- you did not carry out that task because the unit returned to Zadar the next day.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the district court in Zadar, you say that your battalion, around Skabrnja, placed two minefields; one on the north-east where bunkers were dug, and trenches, and where anti-personnel and anti-tank mines were laid. How many mines were involved, do you remember, Mr. Miljanic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have to clarify this matter. I was improvising. I was making mines by using explosives. There were over a hundred where I put explosives and rocks on the explosives, because I was an expert for explosives. So this was done with the intention of preventing any entry into Skabrnja. Because I knew what the Yugoslav People's Army had. So perhaps I had only about ten real anti-tank mines. The rest were these makeshift, improvised minefields made of explosives used for commercial purposes Vitezit, Kamenic [phoen], et cetera, but I did not have any military explosives and I could not put anything else there. That is what I had to say in respect of mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As regards the number, were there over 100? I thought that that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think so, because I put about a kilogram of explosive into every one. A kilogram of explosive, and then I would put rocks all over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: As a military expert, do you think that this is a large quantity of mines?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. I don't think it's a large quantity. I know what minefields are. I myself was wounded by a mine later, and in the former Yugoslav People's Army I dealt with this. This was more of a moral support to my men who had no idea as to what warfare was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During your testimony in the Milosevic case, you mentioned that 1.000 -- that not even the JNA had 1.000 mines.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA had millions of mines. So there you go; millions of mines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Is that what you said in the Milosevic case, the JNA did not even have a thousand?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall. I don't think I stated that, but perhaps it is possible. Maybe I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that that line of defence could not have been crossed by anyone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I stated in my reports in order to give moral support - I repeat that - to my 240 men so that they would remain in the village, so that they would not leave the village, but that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: According to your statement, Mr. Miljanic, the second minefield was near Gradina in Zemunik Donji.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Towards the airfield.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not towards the airfield but above the mental hospital. Not towards the airfield, that's a different direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: There was an airfield in Zemunik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Zadar and Zemunik. This, however, this minefield was between Skabrnja and Zemunik, the one you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, do you know anything about the blockade of the barracks of the JNA in Croatia in that year?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything about that because I left those barracks on my own in a peaceful and dignified way. I said good-bye to everybody and I simply did not run away. I only said I wouldn't stay there, and I left. I don't know anything about what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You don't know anything about the barracks in Zadar and Split?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. As I said, in the police I was just an ordinary pyrotechnician.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, do you know about the many cases of attacks on JNA officers and arrests by the Croatian police and the confiscating of weapons from JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I lived in a building that only military personnel resided in. I chatted to them every day, and in my neighbourhood, nobody underwent such an experience. So I don't think it's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 15th of August 1991, the General Staff of the JNA issued an order that all JNA barracks should have the siege lifted -- just let me finish my question -- by units on territories that were not under threat?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I am not aware of this because I was not a prominent member either of the command of the police in Zadar or the Crisis Staff. I repeat that I was only a pyrotechnician in the Zadar police administration. My position was pyrotechnic inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was Skabrnja one of the points on the route one had to pass to get to the barracks in Zadar and Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the routes, yes, but there is another route leading to Skabrnja, a road that runs from Benkovac through Smiljcic, Gornji Zemunik, the airfield, all the way to Babin Dub, or Crni, and the army was able to move freely along that road. It didn't have to pass through Skabrnja. Nobody passed through Skabrnja anyway because it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But Skabrnja was one of the routes?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was on one of the routes. There was a road, yes. As I said yesterday, Mr. Ratko Mladic used to pass through there. He passed there ten times or more in his vehicle without any escort or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, yesterday and in some of your previous statements, you stated that from the military standpoint, Skabrnja had no significance.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. It had no military significance whatsoever. There were no major facilities there, no military targets, no military fortifications, no strategic importance. It was chosen, in my personal opinion, as a political target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you as a military expert whether, in order to achieve a political goal, it's necessary to raise a force of a thousand infantry men, 28 tanks, with artillery preparation and aviation as well as landing by helicopters, and you spoke of this.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'm no expert. I was just a junior JNA officer, so I was not an important military expert, but I was one of the lower-ranking commanders of the JNA carrying out his duties, a komandir rather than a komandant. Secondly, Your Honours, propaganda played a major role here. That's why such a large force was raised of army, police, or paramilitary units to attack a village; simply to demonstrate force and to show that that was the fate awaiting many. That's my opinion as a former junior officer, because I see no other reason for an attack with such a large force on a village inhabited by only 2.000 people. In Skabrnja, there was no one who was not a native of Skabrnja, either the ZNG or the special police or the Black Shirts, as we were constantly called provocatively over the radio. There were no kind of Ustasha units there. It was only local people from Skabrnja. I myself am a native of Skabrnja and I live there today still.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You said that the road was passable for the JNA because Colonel Mladic used it, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And where was Colonel Mladic going, with what purpose?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know then what his purpose was, but I learned later in the police that Mr. Ratko Mladic was going to negotiate in Hotel Kolovare because of Dean Brener, whom he exchanged for certain Croatian people. I don't know whether they were soldiers or civilians or policemen. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And did the European Community mediate in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know. I wasn't in Zadar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was that the reason why, at that time, Colonel Mladic was able to travel down that road?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was able to travel normally. In that period from Zemunik airport fuel was taken every day in the direction of Benkovac. Tank trucks passed through quite normally, without any hindrance. There was no hindrance to the traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 22nd of September, 1991, an agreement was reached that all JNA garrisons and barracks should have the siege lifted?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not aware of that. Nobody informed me of those things, and there were no barracks in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Not in Skabrnja, but there was a big barracks in Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 14 barracks. Not one; 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, because that's where I did my military service, in Sepurine.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I worked near the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, are you aware that, in spite of this agreement, the JNA barracks in Zadar were exposed to fire by members of the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I wasn't down there. I do have a flat on the boulevard near the railway station, but I didn't go there. I would only come home to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know about the 11 JNA members who were killed in those attacks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really don't know about that because I wasn't in Zadar. I was in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, you said that the attack on Skabrnja began on the 18th of November, 1991, at around 7.30 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And you stated that until 11.30, you were able to hold your ground and that then the line was broken through that was held by the 1st Platoon of the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Miljanic, whether on that day, at around 1100 hours, a unit of about 20 members of the ZNG arrived in your headquarters? They were armed with anti-tank rockets and you sent them to Razovljeva Glavica to shoot at tanks at close range; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At around 1300 hours, you were informed that the defence line from the direction of -- had been broken through from the direction of Marinovci.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to add a correction to what you said previously. 20 members of the ZNG did arrive with six or seven rockets, but they were unable to carry out their task, or they didn't have the courage to do it, and they came back with the job not done, and they left. So there was no attack on tanks, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: But was there an order to attack the tanks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I issued that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on that day, a JNA truck with ammunition exploded.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At the time of the explosion, was this truck in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was overlooking Skabrnja on the Zemunik-Biljane road, the road leading to Benkovac. It was on the road, just above the house where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what caused the explosion of this truck?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was hit or by whom. It was enough for a single rifle bullet to hit a truck full of ammunition to have it explode. Either it was a JNA shell that misfired or I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible that a member of your battalion hit it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, because if it was sufficient to hit it with a rifle bullet or a machine-gun to cause an explosion, then yes, of course, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, yesterday you mentioned, in connection with the conversation you heard concerning that truck with ammunition, that you recognised the voice of Colonel Ratko Mladic because you used to meet him in Knin while you were still in the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I met Ratko Mladic - probably they told me that's who he was - but he wasn't my commander. But of course I recognised him because he was often on television. That was probably another reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you were able to recognise his voice?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to recognise his voice. I know it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: We heard from you that in May 1991, you left the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submitted a request in May 1991. I waited for the decision for a month, and in June I left the JNA. For a month, I waited for the document to come through because I had applied formally to leave the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in July 1991, Ratko Mladic was transferred to Knin from Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So that was a whole two months after you left the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two months? Maybe, probably. I don't know, because as I said, I applied to leave in May -- for permission to leave the JNA, and I left a month later and I went to the Senjak barracks in Knin for the takeover of duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question arises: Did you ever actually meet Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You think you did?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, did the witness not say yesterday that he knew Mr. Mladic's voice because he used to hear him on television, speaking. It's the other guy that he said knew very well, Konkovic or something like that. But he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tripko Cecovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. That's my recollection of the evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm simply trying to remove a dilemma. If in May the witness left his army service and Mladic was transferred to Knin from Macedonia in July of the same year, the question arises whether the witness was able to meet him or come across him at all, as he said he had. The witness answered that he thought he had met Mladic. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, in the evening, you went to Zadar to ask for help; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And on the same evening, you returned to Skabrnja, to the reserve command post?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the evening but in the morning of the 19th. The 19th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that you spent the night between the 18th and the 19th of November, 1991, and that you were holding practically half of Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Night had fallen and because the tanks were old tanks, they were not able to fire at night. They all parked in the centre of the village and all combat activity ceased by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When did you withdraw from the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th November, in the morning - it was around 5.00 - those who had survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you stated that it was truly an unequal situation between you and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So could you please give me an explanation, or rather, give the Trial Chamber an explanation, and to me as well: How did you manage in that kind of situation, it's 24 hours practically, to hold half of Skabrnja in your own hands?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because every man who defends his own home, his own hearth and sees that his mother was killed, his father was killed, his sister, his wife, 85-year-old grandmother, will do his very best and he is not going to surrender just like that. And he is not going to fall into the hands of, not the JNA but the members of those paramilitary units, to be massacred. I have all of it here and I can show you later all the things that happened. But when a man is defending his own home -- my people from Skabrnja did not attack a Serb village or Serb positions. They were defending their homes, and they were being killed at their own doorsteps. So we have to bear that in mind. When you defend your very own, you do your very best, and I did my very best to put a stop to all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that, Mr. Miljanic, you said that those who were reached by the JNA were lucky. On the basis of that, I conclude that the army was not committing crimes; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are traumatic situations. I talked about this to everybody. Talked to my mother, and also my close relatives who survived, and they said to me -- I did not see this, I cannot tell you, Your Honours, that I myself saw this. Had I seen this, I would not be here today. Those who were taken prisoner by the army were taken to trucks and thus saved. But behind the Yugoslav People's Army were the paramilitary units, and they liquidated everyone they came across. That is what I learned from conversations. This is my village. This is where my nearest and dearest are. So I don't know: I'm repeating to the Honourable Trial Chamber, I did not see any of this myself. I was trying to organise things to organise the defence to repel the attack, so I didn't manage to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, I don't want to put questions to you in relation to the crime in Skabrnja itself because, as you say, you were not witness to that crime. However, I want to ask you something. You mentioned a few times the names of certain -- rather the names of Radmanovic, Goran Opacic, nicknamed Klempo, then Mirko Draca, Zorana Banic and her husband Bozo. In relation to that, I would like to ask you the following: Did these persons know each other or were they related in any way, or are these people who did not even know each other?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say. I don't know. Specifically, I knew Zorana Banic very well. I knew her because she was a nurse and she treated my mother. Her husband, I did not know. Then this Radmanovic I knew, because he worked with me in the JNA, Pero Radmanovic. He visited my home many times. Goran Opacic, nicknamed Klempo, I knew from Zadar, but by sight only. So I knew some people, and I didn't know others. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: My question, as I put it, was aimed at clarifying matters, namely whether these people we mentioned were related in any way. Did they constitute an organised group or was every one of them operating on their own?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the question of formations and mutual relations among these people is something that I don't know about. I repeat: I was not friends with these people before because we had different jobs and I was not in touch with them. And after I left the JNA, I did not know what the actual situation was or the formation, the establishment; I don't know who was where. I did not have time, and frankly, I didn't really feel like thinking about things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. Miljanic. Practically to this day, you do not know with full certainty who killed your father.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some indications, collecting information from very different people, and I even received telephone calls as to who it was that had killed my father, so I cannot say even on this day to the Honourable Trial Chamber who it was that killed my -- or massacred my father. My mother said one thing, the wife of my late brother said other things, friends were telling me yet a third thing, the children who were taken prisoner were saying a fourth thing. So it is not with certainty that I can say this to the Honourable Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic. I have no further questions for you. I thank you for the answers that you have provided.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my cross-examination, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, yesterday during cross-examination you mentioned that you were appointed commander for the defence of seven villages and that there were some 700 and something men under your command. Can you give us an idea of the diameter of that area? That is to say the area encompassed by these seven villages.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned these seven villages, that is approximately one-third of the municipality of Zadar, in the heart of Ravni Kotari. 34 kilometres of a line. That is what it was, about 34 kilometres of a line. And that is where these 730 to 740 men were deployed. That was it. Volunteers only. That is to say people who were not members of the Croatian army, or rather, the National Guards Corps but only the reserve police force and volunteers, local villagers. I repeat: It was the territorial principle that was involved. Every village had its own protection. That is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Defence also asked you about weapons at the disposal of you and your men in Skabrnja, and I want to ask you this: Did you have any aircraft at your disposal in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had nothing. I as a soldier, when I was sent up there for three days, as I mentioned yesterday, and then it was extended because nobody wanted to come up there to organise things and to be with these people, it was only me, and I accepted that, we had nothing. Nothing. What do you mean aircraft? What do you mean cannons? Tanks? We had nothing. We were unarmed people. My former JNA -- I was a member of the JNA. Your Honours, I did my service and I served in the JNA. It had disarmed the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Croatia beforehand. And they took the weapons of the Territorial Defence, because before the war, a strong Territorial Defence had been set up in Yugoslavia, and every republic had its own Territorial Defence. Every town had its own brigades, and these weapons were kept by the civilian sector in individual towns. At that time, the JNA, in the beginning of 1991, took away all the weapons of the Territorial Defence, put them in their warehouses, and left the Territorial Defence totally unorganised in Croatia. When I realised what was going on, I left this same JNA. That was the reason. I repeat: I was in the JNA for 22 years. I went to the Ministry of the Interior to do my job, the job that I had been trained for. I note once again to this Honourable Court: I did not provoke in any way this rage that was unleashed on Skabrnja. I did not do it. My people did not do it. Who caused it, I don't know, but what the objective was, I understand up to a point. That is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Miljanic. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Valabhji.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: In the record of your interview on the 5th of October 1992, which you signed, you -- do you agree that you said: "I was sent to organise the defence of Skabrnja and Zemunik Gornji, but since most of this village was populated by Serbs, this effectively boiled down to organising the defence in the hamlet of Istok, populated solely by Croats"? Do you agree that you said that and signed to having said that in your statement of the 5th of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is true. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The defence of Skabrnja that you're speaking about here when you're giving evidence, does it relate solely to the hamlet of Istok or generally to Skabrnja? Could you relate it to the evidence that you've given today, this statement about it boiling down effectively to organising the defence in the hamlet of Istok.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hamlet of Istok is part of Gornji Zemunik. It is a village that is Skabrnja's neighbouring village. It is adjacent to Skabrnja. The western part of Gornji Zemunik, exactly where the main road passes between Smiljcic, the air base, and Zadar is populated by Serbs. And the eastern part, by Croats only. Before the war, they had a common school, and other institutions, shops, the school, et cetera. And all of this, everything I said, pertains only to Skabrnja. And in this eastern part of Gornji Zemunik, there were two platoons, also members -- or rather, people from Gornji Zemunik that were within those 730, 740 people that I had. So it's all of them. At first, I came just to resolve this Skabrnja and Gornji Zemunik, to put things in order. That is what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned sending 80 men who had left the JNA to Zadar. What was in Zadar and where were you sending them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall explain straight away. In Zadar there was a centre, a reception centre, at the Kolovare Hotel, where all people who had defected from the former JNA came to. Some were armed, others did not have weapons. The situation was one of chaos. And then, down there, they would get civilian clothing through the Red Cross, and they were given money for travel tickets, either to Macedonia or Slovenia, Serbia, Kosovo or Croatia, anywhere, anywhere in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and they left. Somebody would get a -- would bring a rifle, somebody would bring a small pack of bullets, other people came without anything. Quite simply, they were fleeing. All ethnicities, everybody who was in the army. There are records of that in the Zadar Red Cross, complete records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Can you say who murdered the police officers at Berevo [phoen]? Was it Serbs or Croats? And the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You had given evidence that there were police officers murdered at Berevo, as I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borovo, Borovo. I understand now, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you if you're aware of who murdered them and the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Borovo is near Vukovar. That's about 400 kilometres away. I don't know who it was and what happened. It was just on television, on television. I can still see the picture clearly in my mind even today. The policemen near Borovo, the JNA was there, around them. Who did what, I don't know. I cannot say anything about this. I just saw this on television.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When you heard that people in the hamlet were being killed and you were told that they were being taken out one by one, what did you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, at that time, I didn't know what to do. I felt like committing suicide. I really wanted to kill myself. I felt like killing myself when I saw all of that, experienced all of that, when people who had come to see me five minutes before that, got killed, I felt like taking a pistol and killing myself, and then people said, "Marko, don't. All of this will blow over, perhaps it will be stopped," but that's the way I felt, because, Your Honour, to this day -- well, nobody is blaming me, my local villagers, no one. I worked honestly. I didn't do anything to provoke anybody. But still, I feel this to be part of my own conscience. My parents, my brother, my relatives, everybody, and that 97-year-old lady who was massacred here although she had had a stroke, and all of these people who were killed in my Skabrnja, who were run over by tanks. What came to the pathology department were kilograms and kilograms of meat. After this trial, I will not be able to come to for a month, Your Honour. These are such horrible things. It is very, very hard for me to speak about this, although I'm an old soldier. I have been through all sorts of things but I never thought that I would experience something like that, Your Honour. I'm not accusing anyone. I'm not here to accuse anyone. I am just presenting the facts, the facts that I know. Who is guilty, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned that the army went through and then the vultures passed. Now, I understand you mean by the vultures the paramilitary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. I don't know what the composition was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Were you advised how these people were dressed?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I didn't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that at 4.00 -- sorry, 14 hours, there were civilians around the tanks that prevented you from shooting. Do you know how they got to be around the tanks?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not see. Well except for these tanks and these civilians, but when I talked to all of these people of mine, they said that they were getting them out of basements and they were afraid that somebody could shoot at the tanks so they used them as a human shield in front of the tanks. Now, who it was that did that - the JNA or the paramilitaries - I don't know that to this day and I cannot say. But when they came into the centre of the village around 1400 hours, I really had the intention to destroy at least one tank with a hand-held rocket launcher, but when I saw these civilians, I withdrew and I did not want to shoot. I had put a shell there and I wanted to shoot but I was afraid that they would all be killed. Fortunately, all of these people survived, and most of them still live in Skabrnja, those people who were there when I did not shoot. Now, who it was that saved them, and what happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, you said that 15 or 16 people were killed - of that group of 242, I understood that to mean - that 14 were taken prisoner. What became of the rest?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, and the following two or three days, I did not know at all how many people had been killed. I did not know. I did not know whether my father had really gotten killed or whether he was taken somewhere, whether he was taken prisoner. I didn't know about my brother, whether he was killed and whether he was captured or whatever. My mother, who is 85 today, was looking for her son. She saw her husband and she said, yes, son, they killed him, but I only saw her a few days later. She said to me, They killed your father, and things like that. But as for the others, I didn't know. I didn't know. Amongst all the fire and everything, I didn't know. I only knew about the people who got killed right next to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now you mentioned Petar Radmanovic. What ethnic group was he?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you mentioned - please excuse my pronunciation - Mr. Miljus, who conducted the on-site investigation. What position did he hold in the police administration in Benkovac and what ethnic group did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Mr. Miljus only superficially while in Zadar. I did not know him personally. I'm not claiming that he was the one who carried out the on-site investigation, but in the documents that were captured during Operation Storm, where there were pictures of all these massacres, there was a stamp of the police station in Benkovac, and underneath the signature was Dragan Miljus. I think he was a Serb, I don't know, I don't know at all what the man's ethnic background was. I heard from people that he was a crime technician in the police. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Next -- just -- this is the final question now. What municipality is Sabrinska [phoen] in?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been to Saborsko. It is somewhere in Gorski Kotar. Saborsko is in Gorski Kotar. I don't know. I was never there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have said Skabrnja. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, Skabrnja. Skabrnja belonged to the municipality of Zadar. Skabrnja is the municipality of Zadar, part of the municipality of Zadar. Today, it is an independent municipality, the municipality of Skabrnja, but before the war it was the municipality of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Miljanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Mr. Miljanic, you mentioned that on the 2nd of October, 1991, after the attack, some people were evacuated from the village of Skabrnja. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who evacuated these people?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross, the Zadar Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where were they evacuated to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Dugi Otok, an island, and an island called Ugljan, which is about 15 miles down from Zadar. It's in the Adriatic Sea, facing Italy. So Zadar, then there is the islands in the Adriatic Sea. So they were taken there by ferry and they were put up in hotels on these islands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How long were they there for?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the way up to the 5th of November, when the cease-fire in The Hague was signed. And when I was told about this, because I had not known about it, by Mr. Ivan Brzoja, chief of the Zadar police administration, these were his words: Everybody is coming back, a cease-fire was signed in The Hague between the JNA and -- I don't know, the JNA -- I don't know who it was that signed this cease-fire at all, but it was signed in The Hague and I received these orders in writing, and that all my civilians should return to the village. And that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When these people returned on the 5th of November, they returned back to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To their village, to their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying when the attack started again on the 18th of November, these people were back in the village?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, the 18th. It was from the 5th, when The Hague cease-fire was signed, until the 18th, there was peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. On the 18th, there was violence?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An attack, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was simply: These people who had been evacuated to the island were back in the village when the attack started again on the 18th of November. Am I right in saying so?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were sent back on the 5th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When, in your evidence, you made a reference to people being killed one by one in your hamlet, were you referring to Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Skabrnja. Fortunately, I didn't go to other places, but unfortunately, I was in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have testified, both in your evidence-in-chief and during cross-examination, about the paramilitary that you say were killing people everywhere. This morning, actually, under cross-examination, you said that it was not the JNA but the members of those paramilitary units who massacred the people. What was the name of this paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot define it simply. Was it the Territorial Defence? Was it the milicija, the SAO Krajina Police? I don't know who it was. But those who saw them, according to what they say, they were all masked, but there were even 12- or 13-year-old children. My mother told me, that a 13-year-old boy beat her with a rifle butt. Who he belonged to, I really don't know, because -- let me just say the following: Even in wartime, there are telephone lines. While I was serving, I was called all kinds of names. I was told that I was an Ustasha, and I repeat to this Honourable Court that I don't know who the Ustasha were. I was not alive at the time. My father did not participate in World War II. He was a 14-year-old boy at the time. I know nothing about that. I repeat to this Honourable Chamber that I tried to avoid this evil, but I was not successful in that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, we, the Bench, the Chamber, sympathises and feels with you in the experiences that you went through but, unfortunately we have to ask these questions, and if you will just bear with us a little while longer. Do you know if that paramilitary unit was wearing a specific uniform?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they wore military -- the old military uniforms belonging to the JNA. In their activities, some wore camouflage uniforms and others wore solid colour uniforms, but I don't know who was who. In that chaos, it was impossible to know. I cannot confirm something I did not see. But according to what the soldiers who fled from the JNA, who left the JNA, say, they all told me to watch out because there were lots of Chetniks - that was the term they used - who had come to take their places in the JNA and who would not forgive us. I don't know what there was not to be forgiven, what we had done, but they told us, watch out, they are going to -- they are going to erase you off the face of the earth. But I didn't believe that. I thought it was just stories to frighten children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Miljanic. We have to take a short break and we'll carry on when we come back at quarter to 11. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Miljanic, just before we went for the break, you said that these paramilitaries were referred to as Chetniks. What did you understand the word "Chetniks" to mean?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I have read about this - because I have never seen a Chetnik - but I heard that in World War II they were subordinate units composed of Serbs who had their own ideology, probably they had their own chain of command. It was a kind of party army, as had probably existed in Croatia also, and these were called Ustasha. I have never seen them either, but I heard that those were units waging war on behalf of a certain nation. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that some of these paramilitaries wore camouflage uniform and others wore a one-colour uniform. Did the one-colour uniform they wore differ from the one worn by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The one-colour, olive-grey uniforms were uniforms worn by soldiers of the JNA, which I also served in, as I have already said. These other uniforms, especially these camouflage uniforms, belonged to certain elite units, special purpose units, at least while I was serving in the former JNA. As the Yugoslav People's Army also had a Territorial Defence, these JNA uniforms were probably kept by certain people who put them on at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You also testified yesterday that all the people who were taken prisoner were killed, and you said these were civilians. Do you have an idea of the number?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat: I don't know when someone was killed and on what day. About 25, 26 or 27 civilians stayed behind in Skabrnja after it was occupied. They were alive until February 1992, when they were all killed; and later on, they were exhumed from a mass grave in the centre of the village. Who killed them, and who buried them, is something I don't know. But in 1995, the mass grave was opened up and 27 corpses were found. One was a soldier and the others were all civilians, 25 or 26 civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1991, when the attack took place, do you have an idea how many people were killed on that day, how many civilians were killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know for certain - and I didn't see it myself but I heard it from my mother and the people who were there - is when my father was killed, and certain other people. I know that in that hamlet at the entrance to Skabrnja, about 20 civilians were killed. I don't know the precise number, but about 20. Among them, the oldest person who was killed on that day was 96 years old. Her name was Grgica Segaric. She was my next door neighbour. She had had a stroke and she was bedridden. They came and they killed her. She was brought to the forensic institute. My mother described how she saw them kill my father and other people, but I was not there myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I notice you raise a paper there with you. And this is not the first time you are raising it up this morning. Is it a paper that you want the Court to see?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was brought from the pathology unit. It was done by the Medecins Sans Frontieres after the massacres in Skabrnja and Nadin. And my colleagues from the police dealt with this so they kept a copy for me. I gave it to the lady from the Office of the Prosecutor, and if you are interested in it, I can let Your Honours see it. These are terrible pictures. Among them is a picture of my father and all the others. And here you will also see members of the OSCE observing all this in front of the mortuary. I can let you see it, if you wish, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps if I may, I do have a copy of this. The witness kindly provided it to us. I had thought, actually, that it might be discussed through another witness, who will also be testifying later on regarding exhumations and the pathology work. However, I'm happy to, at this time, provide to the Bench this copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have a copy to provide to your opposite number?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: This is a colour copy, Your Honour, and actually, the Defence has a copy of this document. It was disclosed to them. Perhaps they don't have it at the present time. Now, I have a black and white copy as well. This is a black and white copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, do you have any objection to the Bench having a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no objection to the Bench looking at the document in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. May it be admitted into evidence? Or shall it wait its turn, as Mrs. Valabhji says?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that would be the best solution, at the proposal of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be absolutely fine to have it admitted into evidence at the present time, and should it warrant further discussion through another witness later on, that can also be done and the admitted exhibit at that time can be referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The only reason I'm following it up is because Mr. Miljanic is raising it a second time and I thought that it was something he wants us to see in this document. Would you like to say anything about this paper, Mr. Miljanic? Or are you happy that it be discussed through another witness later?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am very satisfied with your proposal that an expert say something about this document. I'm only a lay person. I only have photographs, nothing else. So it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In that event, then, if the Prosecutor decides to hand it in through another witness, the Chamber will look at it at that stage. Is that okay? Thank you very much. Do you know why Petar Radmanovic provoked you in the manner in which he did, as you explained yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no reason for it. I don't. We had been good friends. He had been to my home a dozen times and more. He was a neighbour from a neighbouring village, Gornje Biljane. I saw no reason for him to be so bitter towards me, so angry, and why he said all those things to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yesterday you described Mr. Opacic -- I hope I'm pronouncing it correctly, O-p-a-c-i-c -- as an SAO Krajina Police. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this from others. I knew him from before the war, from Zadar, but not well. I had met Mr. Opacic. We all knew each other more or less in Zadar, to some extent, and all I know about him is that he left the Zadar police, and I don't know when that was. Where he was and what duties he performed, I don't know, but according to some information I have, he was probably one of the commanders of a platoon or a company or something like that, but I don't really know what his role was. When Mr. Radmanovic called me on the radio, those civilians were there who knew him better than I did said, "That's Klempo." I don't know whether he was Klempo or not. And I really don't know what his role in all this was. I cannot say things that I only heard by hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you from arising out of your description of Mr. Opacic is whether, to your knowledge, SAO Krajina police participated with the JNA in this operation.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true. I repeat, Your Honours: From my experience as a policeman and a soldier, I know that they participated. Because these were all neighbours of ours, people who would visit Skabrnja in their official capacity. They had been in the old police. Later it changed its name, both in Croatia and everywhere else. It was no longer called the Milicija but the Policija, and the inhabitants of Skabrnja knew these people because it all belonged to the Zadar police station, and these people had been employees in that police station. I didn't see any of them personally. Had I seen them I would not be alive here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm going to have to ask my question again because I'm not getting -- I don't think I understood you clearly. Is your answer yes, there were SAO Krajina Police?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, there was an investigation that you say was conducted by Mr. Miljus on behalf of the police administration. Which police administration is this on whose behalf he conducted the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the stamp in this study, because a study is always compiled, it said, "Milicijska Stanica Benkovac," which means "Benkovac Police Station," Benkovac. And that shows for what police Mr. Miljus was working. Whether they had conducted an investigation or not, I don't know, but this study or report always had a stamp under the picture, and it said, "Benkovac Police Station." At that time, that was part of the SAO Krajina. Benkovac was part of the SAO Krajina all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. What is a pyrotechnician? What does a pyrotechnician do in the police?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every police has its pyrotechnicians. They are the people who search us when we enter this Tribunal to see whether we are carrying an explosive device. At the airport, all packages and letters are examined by pyrotechnicians, and I was the chief of the department of this kind in the Zadar police administration. I had six pyrotechnicians who did that every day. The other thing we did, because at that time the Croatian army did not have its pyrotechnicians, so every shell that was fired but did not explode in the town, I had to go with my men and I had to remove it and destroy it. I was an expert for explosives and anti-sabotage protection, which means protection against terrorism. This is done by every country and police in the world. That's what I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. A question I'm going to ask you may be a little difficult to answer but to the best of your ability, please do try, if you can. Are you able to give an idea of the extent of destruction of the village of Skabrnja? Was the whole village destroyed? Only part of it? Or are you able to give numbers?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in Skabrnja, up until the 19th of November, a certain number of houses in Skabrnja had been destroyed, buildings including the school and the church, because the planes of the Yugoslav People's Army dropped cassette bombs, cluster bombs, on Skabrnja, and these cluster bombs are banned by the Geneva Convention. They left little bombs behind. At that time, 30 or 40 per cent of the houses were destroyed. Later on, I personally entered Skabrnja with the UNPROFOR in 1994. I was permitted by UNPROFOR to accompany them. They were members of the Canadian Battalion. They took me along and at that time, 90 or maybe even 95 per cent of Skabrnja had been destroyed. In the investigation I gave the names of the houses and what category of damage they had suffered; first, second, third or fourth. This classification was carried out after the liberation so that those houses that had been destroyed in the war could be rebuilt. Most of the houses fell into the fifth category of destruction, which means they had been razed to the ground. This had not been done by projectiles and shells but by the planting of explosives and blowing the houses up. The church was destroyed down to the foundations. We have now built a new one. All the important facilities in Skabrnja had been destroyed. There had been three churches in Skabrnja; the main one was completely destroyed, the other two were badly damaged. Everything else was damaged or destroyed. There was a very small number of buildings that fell into the first category of damage, which meant they could be repaired and lived in. That was the situation in Skabrnja. Who destroyed those houses or why, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mentioned cluster bombs being used. Do I understand by "cluster bombs" that you mean that this whole cluster of them that are thrown without aiming them at a specific target? I see you nod your head. Would you like to say in a voice what you mean by nodding your head, because unfortunately, if you nod your head, the transcript doesn't record the nodding.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true. Cluster bombs, I saw them for the first time in 1991, when they were activated. They were carried by planes, and they consist of 240 smaller bombs in a casing, and 40 per cent explode right away, as soon as they touch the ground, whereas 60 per cent remain inactivated or on a patch about 200 by 50 metres and these are used then to destroy living creatures; human beings, animals and so on. These are terrorist weapons. Such bombs were thrown on Skabrnja from planes. This was mentioned in the newspapers and on television, and European observers came to photograph this, in 1991, before Skabrnja fell. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did Skabrnja fall, exactly? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Miljanic. Any questions, Ms. Valabhji, arising from the questions from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Just one point, Your Honour. I was wondering if it might be possible to show the witness admitted Exhibit 270, arising out of the questioning concerning the investigation in Benkovac, to see if he recognises that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Is it displayed now? If we could go to page 3. Witness, are you able to view page 3 of this document on your screen? Can we also then turn to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. I see it says documentation of on-site inspection. That is the document found in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document of the inspection -- the investigation, and this stamp was there, underneath every photograph. This is the kind of photographic documentation compiled by a police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Valabhji. Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miljanic, today when asked by Her Honour, you explained that the paramilitaries that followed the JNA and committed crimes were composed of people whom you didn't know who they were or how they were dressed because you didn't see any of them. Let me just finish my question. A little later, when asked by His Honour Judge Moloto, you said that some of the eye witnesses told you that these people were masked and that, according to what you know, they wore old military uniforms which had previously belonged to the former JNA, but that you couldn't confirm this because you didn't see them personally. And finally, in your statement given to the district court in Zadar, on page 6, in the third paragraph, you say that, I quote: "I was unable to recognise any of those Chetniks because they all had black paint on their faces and some had stockings or socks over their heads and some had white ribbons on their shoulders."

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: That is your statement to the Zadar district court, and it's on page 6, paragraph 3. Let me finish my question. It seems to me that between these three replies, your reply to Her Honour Judge Nosworthy, your reply to His Honour Judge Moloto, and your statement given to the district court in Zadar, there are certain discrepancies. Can you explain them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said, and I abide by this, that I did not see anybody. But if my mother tells me that she recognised Mr. Desimir Ivanez, a member of the then police, Milicija of SAO Krajina, I have to believe her. Another man called him by his name, and he responded, saying, "If you use my name once again, I'll kill you like a dog." I didn't see it myself but my mother told me this. I knew Desimir Ivanez personally. As for the white ribbons, I saw those because they had them when they were coming to the school. Who was wearing white ribbons, I don't know, but when I had to carry out the task of destroying that tank, I did see white ribbons on their left shoulder. But I did not know any of them, so I cannot confirm to Their Honours about any particular person, that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: May I then conclude that you are unable to identify the men you describe as paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm this because I did not see it myself. I can believe my mother and my relatives, but then I don't have to believe them. I can only say what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question: You said that in Skabrnja it was peaceful in the period between the 5th and the 18th of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In relation to that I have a question. Why, then, on the 16th of November, on the 16th of November, were you planning an action with a unit for special purposes of the MUP of Croatia under the command of a certain Djuro Zupan? So why were you planning with them to destroy the tank group of the JNA in Veljun --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljane.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: -- Veljane, if the situation was peaceful at the time, as you said?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First and foremost, I did not plan that. Because Djuro Zupan came to Skabrnja without my knowledge, but I had agreed with him verbally for a simple reason, the most important one, a single reason, because, I repeat: Soldiers were fleeing from the JNA. And they told me that all tank crews - because they fled from tanks - all tank crews consisted of volunteers from Serbia and local people, and that they would attack me. And I wanted to do this by way of prevention. I didn't succeed in doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Further questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber what was the significance of the white ribbons?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is done during the war so that you would not kill your own soldier in smoke, when visibility is limited. So in smoke, fire, when you cannot hear a voice, and then some use white ribbons in order to have a mark of distinction, and some use other colours, depending on the units. But that is how they recognise each other so that they would not harm each other, because that is very likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: My next question, then, is who would wear the white ribbon, who in particular? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MILJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, this action probably, in my personal opinion, was planned jointly by the JNA with the staff of the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina, or I don't know who, but probably, because they went together, so this coordination probably existed. And all units that attack a particular place at a given time -- it's not only what the then-JNA did. That is being done to this day in wars. There has to be some mark of distinction so that people do not kill each other. That is how they recognise each other. We didn't have that because we didn't have uniforms anyway. We wore civilian clothes. I'm the only one who had a complete police uniform. And a few other men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that unusual procedure. Any questions arising from those questions by Judge Nosworthy, Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Miljanic, thank you so much. We thank you for coming to testify. We -- everybody has asked what we wanted to ask of you. You are now excused and you may stand down. Thank you very much once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you, and it was a pleasure for me to tell this Honourable Court the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Valabhji?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
