utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be handled by my colleague Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: And may I have the Court's permission in withdrawing at this time, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you withdrawing from the case or are you withdrawing from the court building?

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: From the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are allowed to withdraw from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. VALABHJI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you call the next witness, can we deal with a little housekeeping matter? Apparently Registry has a little problem tomorrow in terms of staff, and as a result, we are being asked to make some slight changes to our sitting tomorrow. We have been asked to sit from nine to 20 past 10 instead of quarter past 10 -- let me preface this. At some stage, the Court officer is going to be required to do some work elsewhere and there is nobody to replace him in this Court, and the only way we can accommodate that is if we would be in a position to sit from 9 to 20 past 10, and then reconvene at 10 to 11 and then break at 10 past 12 instead of 12.00, because at 10 past 12 he's got to be somewhere else. And then we can break from 10 past until 20 to 1 and, having come at 20 to 1, then we could go up to quarter to 2 as usual. Would that be okay with everybody? Let's find out from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There is no problem on our side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On your side, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We agree, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I caught the Judges also by surprise. I'm sure it would be -- thank you very much. And everybody else, I'm sure? Okay. Thank you so much, then we will sit according to those times tomorrow, then. Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Mr. Hamdija Krupic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness was formerly granted protective measures but yesterday he informed the OTP that he will testify in open session without any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. You may sit down, Mr. Krupic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you follow the proceedings in a language you can understand?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Good morning. I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you please tell your full name.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Hamdija Krupic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, did you provide a witness statement, or better say two witness statements; one on 22 August 1999 and the second one on the 19 July 2000?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Regarding the first statement of 22nd of August, 1999, on 10 of November, 2001, did you have occasion to review this statement in the presence of the officer of the Court and did you sign a declaration, declaration attesting to its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Referring to the statement of 19 July 2000, on 29 March 2006, which is yesterday, did you go through the same procedure that -- in front of an officer of the Court; you reviewed your statement and then signed declaration attesting that statement?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Krupic's witness statements were admitted into evidence by Trial Chamber's decision dated 16 of January 2006, under Rule 92 bis, and we, as indicated at the decision, we made redactions. We already gave hard copies of these statements to the Defence counsel, and I have -- I brought hard copies for Your Honours, just in case you want to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to tender these two statements into evidence, and I would like to get an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Have they not already been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: They haven't been admitted officially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Officially, okay. May the statements be admitted into evidence and be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There are two statements. It will have to be 279 maybe for the statement of the 22nd of August, 1999, and 280 for the statement of the 19th of July 2000.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be -- Exhibit number 280, Your Honours, for the second statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to usual procedure for Rule 92 bis statements, I will read the summary of the statement and afterwards I would have a -- have some follow-up questions before I hand over the witness for cross-examination. Before I begin my summary, I would like to direct the Trial Chamber to the map, to atlas, Exhibit 23, to page 21, and you will see Bosanski Novi, which is the town about which the witness will testify, in grid C3. And on the same map, you will also -- on the same grid, you will also see other places which are mentioned in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi, yes. I will now begin the summary. The witness is a Bosnian Muslim who lived in Bosanski Novi and he worked as a policeman. According to census, there was a slight majority of Serbs living in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. There was a JNA barracks in Bosanski Novi before the war in Croatia, however, the unit moved out before the start of the war and they moved to Croatia and the unit of Territorial Defence and JNA reservists moved in. Kosta Djukic was their commander. The SDS won the elections in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Witness stated that he attended at least one of the SDS rallies where the mayor of Bosanski Novi, a Serb, Radomir Pasic, spoke. Mr. Pasic used sharp words, stating that Serbs were in jeopardy from Ustashas and that they, Serbs, had to defend themselves. After the elections, a Serb, Djuro Umicevic, became or, better say, continued to be the chief of police. In witness's words, he was a fair man, supporting united police forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interrupt you? You said after the elections, a Serb --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry? I said that a Serb, a Serb person named Djuro Umicevic became the chief of police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's all right. Umicevic? You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Umicevic was killed during a conflict among Serbs in a bar sometimes in February or March 1992. After the elections, the cooperation between SDS and SDA, which was the Muslim party, was good. However, once the war started in Croatia and Muslims refused to be mobilised to fight in Croatia, the ethnic tensions became higher. Also, the police force reserve was mobilised. The witness says that at the beginning of the war in Croatia, there was lots of propaganda which heated up the tension between Serbs and Muslims. Railways had to be secured as explosives were being planted. The blowing up of railways started with the log revolution in Knin, and the same things then were happening in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. At the end of 1991 or beginning of 1992, Muslim-owned houses and businesses started to be targeted with explosives. Serbs in the municipality were receiving openly weapons. The witness says that the separation of police forces started in Bosanska Krupa and Hrvatska Kostajnica. After Hrvatska Kostajnica fell into the hands of Serbs, the witness was present when members Croat MUP were crossing the bridge. These policemen were disarmed, weapons were put on pile, and the local Bosnian Serbs would take these weapons away. The witness says that members of special police from Knin were present during this disarmament. Sometime at the end of 1991 or at the beginning of 1992, a special unit from Banja Luka called Red Berets arrived to Bosanski Novi. They wore green camouflage uniforms and wore red berets. They said that their task would be to disarm extremists of all nationalities but they were disarming only Bosniaks. The witness says that some people were arrested, referring to Muslims, and taken to Gradiska and Cerkezovac, which is in Croatia. After the death of Umicevic, the chief of the police, another Serb, Dejan Samara, arrived from Banja Luka. His task was either to separate police along the ethnic lines or force everyone to wear Serb insignia. At the time, Serbs took over all the power and authority in the municipality of Bosanski Novi. On 15 of April 1992, all policemen were invited and asked to sign a loyalty to Serb authorities. The witness refused. The Serbs were issued new camouflage uniforms with Serb flag on the shoulders. These were same uniforms as the special police in Belgrade wore. The witness left the municipality in May 1992. He returned only after the end of the war. The places which he visited after the war were destroyed; all the mosques at these places were destroyed, and he says that none of the Muslim-owned businesses or houses survived. This completes the summary. Now I would have just a few follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, can you assist the Judges and tell them how far is Bosanski Novi to -- how far it is from Bosanski Novi to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Bosanski Novi is separated from Croatia only by the Una River. Dvor Na Uni is only four kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how these two places are connected?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: These two places are connected with a bridge over the Una River.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us how the war in Croatia affected the life in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: In fact, when war broke out in Croatia, it started in Bosanski Novi too because members of the Serb forces wore -- carried rifles in Bosanski Novi and every night there was shooting in town as if it were the front line. The participants in the war were the Serbs from Bosanska Krajina. All of them in the TO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were there also present some armed groups which would come from the Croatian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, from the Croatian Krajina, they came every day. They crossed the bridge and they came to the town of Bosanski Novi where they got drunk and there was shooting in town. And the late chief was killed during such a shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you able to identify what kinds of armed groups came from Croatian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: There were members of the TO, from the so-called Serb Krajina, Martic's Police, and active army personnel while they were in the territory of Cerkezovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were also Martic's Police. How did you know that they were Martic's Police?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, they were called Martic's Police after Martic. This was a secret that everybody knew. They were supposed to be public security but they were trained only for carrying out terrorist attacks and intimidating the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know where they were trained?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that you saw them often in Bosanski Novi. What did they wear?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms with white belts for the most part, and they were often seen. As a matter of fact, they took part in looting when the members of the MUP in Bosanska Kostajnica surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Apart from looting, what -- how -- what else did you know they did in -- on the territory of Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they threw an explosive device at the house of journalist Safic because three men were seen in camouflage uniforms and white belts, and that belonged to Martic's Police. The explosive device was thrown at that house because Safic was an independent journalist who reported impartially from the front line, from SAO Krajina. And another explosive device was thrown at the flower shop of Gazic Zejneba.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was anybody identified or was anybody charged ever with planting of explosive on these two houses?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No one could have been identified because at that time there was a vacuum, in fact. There was a lack of power and authority. The active police that I was a member of could not do their job because they would be killed if they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned on what kind of uniforms they wore. Are you able to tell the Judges what kinds of weapons the members of this group had in their possession?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, they mostly had automatic rifles and pistols, not taking into account the unit that was called the Red Berets. They were armed with MK small calibre weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that they were called Martic's Police because of Martic. Did you know Milan Martic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Not personally. Perhaps I saw him towards the end of 1991 and in 1992 when he passed through Bosanski Novi, and I know that he stopped at the Libertas restaurant in Bosanski Novi. And I saw him when he was released from Otoka, when he was brought to the police station in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that when he was released from Otoka. Can you tell us when it was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly but I think it was the end of 1991, beginning of 1992, because I know that the late chief, Umicevic, was still alive then. Martic was detained in Bosanska Otoka and, at the intervention of the Deputy Minister of the Interior Abdo Habib, he was released from Otoka and brought to the police station in Bosanski Novi in an official vehicle and he was in the late Chief Umicevic's office, and then the owner of this restaurant Libertas, Mile Grbic, came. And from there, Mr. Martic was transferred to the small soccer playing field near the school and then was taken by helicopter in a direction unknown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you saw Milan Martic stop at the Libertas restaurant. Did he visit this restaurant on one or more occasions?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I think that Milan Martic visited that restaurant more than once. He was the only civilian. When Martic was brought from Otoka the only civilian from the area who came to see him was the owner of that restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Talking again about this restaurant, did you know who he met in that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the names, but I do know, because I was the leader of the patrol sector for Bosanski Novi, and I know that that restaurant was often locked at night and was full of guests, members of the former JNA, the command from the former -- from the SAO Krajina, and that they were members of the SDS there and people from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were people from the command of SAO Krajina. Can you name someone?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No. The only person I knew personally was Kosta Djukic, who was the commander of the garrison at Cerkezovac, he was an active duty soldier, because his son Sasa worked with me. He was a communications man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was anyone from the Serb leadership from Bosanski Novi present at that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Every evening, there was a gathering of the extreme part of the SDS from Bosanski Novi there. In the evenings, when I was on duty, I would write down the licence plates of the cars parked there because the door was locked and we couldn't get inside, and at that time already there was separation going on in the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And from these licence plates, were you able to identify who was present?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, it was known. And later it turned out, for example, the late Stole Skundric, who was a tradesman, a neighbour of mine, just an ordinary man, but he was appointed commander of the defence of the town, later on. And he would always go there, to that restaurant, after it was officially closed, when they had their talks inside.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that at least on one occasion you saw Milan Martic. Did you see or are you aware about the presence of someone else from the leadership from Croatian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: The late Milan Babic would come there. He even walked around the town in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the relationship between the Serb leadership of Bosanska Krajina and Croatian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: At that time, I think it was one and the same Krajina, indicating that the Serb population in the Territorial Defence from both sides were in the war together. Politically and materially and morally they were interconnected. For that purpose, in the municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina, on the agendas of the meetings was the founding of so-called Serb municipalities, which were to be joined up to the ones in the SAO Krajina to form a single territory. There was no difference between the Krajina in Bosnia and the SAO Krajina. Practically, there was no border between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that you saw policemen from MUP in Hrvatska Kostajnica walking across the bridge. When was it that Hrvatska Kostajnica fled -- fell?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know the exact date but I think it was late 1991 or early 1992. The representatives of the independent trade union of the republican MUP of the time were in Bosanska Krupa, where the police was divided, and on their way back from Bosanska Krupa they dropped by to see me in Bosanski Novi because I was a member of the republican trade union, and we heard that on that day the MUP men from Hrvatska Kostajnica were in Bosanska Kostajnica. I was in the delegation that went to see what this looked like. But when we arrived in Bosanska Kostajnica there was a sight to behold: Night had already fallen and the members of the Croatian MUP were crossing the bridge one by one, and to the right of the bridge they threw down their long weapons and their pistols, and there they were received by Martic's Policemen. I recognised Ivanovic or Popovic. His first name was Goran, I'm not sure whether he was Ivanovic or Popovic, and they took him to a place that was either a cinema or some kind of community centre nearby, where they took their gold jewellery and watches and such things, and then on the next day, they were put on buses and taken to the camp in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that Martic's men were present. What was their role?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Their role was to take over these members of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia and to search them. The civilian police of Bosanski Novi was also there and I saw some colleagues of mine --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the names.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: -- and the former chief was there but they were there only for show. They weren't actually doing anything. All the actual work was being done by Martic's Police, and they were the ones who robbed those people. And what's very important to mention: About 300 men surrendered, and as they threw their weapons down on the pile, the local Serbs took the weapons, slung them over their backs, and left. So that only about 10 barrels were brought to the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krupic, the interpreter missed one name. You mentioned that a colleague of yours from the police of Bosanski Novi was present, and you stated his name, but we didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Ljubomir Predojevic, Zoran Baskot, and the late chief, Umicevic. There were also other members of the civilian police from Bosanski Novi but right now I cannot recall their names. I was in the civilian section.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you stated that they were taken, the Croat policemen, were taken on buses and put on buses and taken to Manjaca, was still Martic's Police present when they were put on the buses?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That night, I went home together with the colleagues from the republican MUP, but on the following day, at around 10 or 11, I saw the buses going from the direction of Kostajnica towards Prijedor. They were passing through Bosanski Novi, and I saw those people on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I assume -- you didn't answer my question. In fact, what exactly was the Martic's role in this operation? I'm sorry, Martic's Police's role?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: The role of Martic's Police was to take over and search the policemen who -- from the MUP of Croatia who had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see how they treated these Croatian policemen?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: It was night. I personally didn't see it. But on the next day I heard from my colleague Predojevic, who was telling everyone that they took everything from them, they robbed them of every valuable they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krupic. I concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. Mr. Krupic, it's time to take a break. We will come back at half past 12. Please come back. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic. Before you start, Mr. Milovancevic, let me remind you that in terms of the 92 bis ruling, this witness is supposed to be cross-examined only on the matter relating to the Red Berets. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I am Defence counsel for Milan Martic. My name is Predrag Milovancevic. Now is the stage of your testimony that is called cross-examination. I will put questions to you which in our view are of importance for the Defence. I ask you to make a pause between my question and your answer so that the interpreters can do their job. Today, you confirmed that you made two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor and today you answered a series of questions by the Prosecutor. Are these matters that you spoke about to the Office of the Prosecutor during your interview and when you made your statements?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence is faced with a problem of which we wish to inform the Chamber. About 80 to 90 per cent of the responses the witness gave today are absent in his written statements. The Defence has heard them for the first time today. The accused has the right to be informed of what he's being charged with and what the testimony will contain. We now have a real problem here. Almost all the questions to which the witness responded during his examination-in-chief contained facts which are not mentioned in the written statements. The Defence considers this to be a serious issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your learned friend wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with Mr. Milovancevic. The witness mentioned certain issues yesterday during the proofing. I prepared additional information sheet. I sent it to the Defence. And I'm of the opinion that they should be allowed to cross-examine the witness based on this new information I sent them yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you're obviously entitled to cross-examine the witness on those issues that were raised today during questions, in addition to cross-examining him on the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I do, Your Honour, I wish to inform the Chamber that as of the 29th of March 2006, we received a submission by the Prosecutor where three brief sentences are provided as an addition to the witness's statement. However, today, the witness brought up a number of new facts which the Defence has heard for the first time today. In this situation, I ask the Chamber to have the possibility of questioning the witness about these in order to avoid misunderstandings. I do not wish to be criticised for contravening Your Honour's decision on the matters to be brought up in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. As the Chamber has just indicated, you may cross-examine the witness on the questions that were raised this morning by the Prosecution in addition to the questions that you're entitled to ask relating to the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, today the Prosecutor read out a summary of your two statements, and stated a fact, inter alia, that I would like to ask you about, that is whether it originates from you, and that is the composition of the population in Bosanski Novi. The Prosecutor said that there was a slight Serb majority. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Probably in my statement I said there were more Serbs, however, according to the census of 1990 or 1991, there were 37 per cent Bosniaks, 0.05 per cent Croats, and 0.05 per cent others, I think, and the remainder of the population was Serb. I'm referring to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You told us now that there were 37 per cent Bosniaks, whereas in your written statement it says 34 per cent. Which is correct; 34 or 37 per cent?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: It depends on how we look at it, because those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs included a number of Muslims. Whether it's 34 or 37 per cent, in my view, it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying that in relation to the percentage of Muslims and Croats and Yugoslavs, there were 60 per cent Serbs in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, it says that in Bosanski Novi, multi-party elections were held and that there were two main parties; the SDA, the Party of Democratic Action, led by Alija Izetbegovic, and SDS, the Serb Democratic Party. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. The SDA was not only Alija Izetbegovic's party; it was the party of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, it says that according to a previous agreement, there was a situation in which these two parties appointed the leading people in the municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, based on the results of the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, it says that the chief of the SUP of Bosanski Novi, at the initiative of the SDA, the person who was appointed was Umicevic, who was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Umicevic. By Their Honours' leave, I think I should clarify this a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you seem to have described this detail in your written statement.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Azemir Ceric was the police commander and that his name was put forward by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The SDA is the Party of Democratic Action, the party you say that was the party of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to repeat: Please make a pause between question and answer, to avoid overlapping. In your statement, it says that the SDS initially did everything in agreement with the SDA. Therefore, the Serb Democratic Party did everything in agreement with the Party of Democratic Action in Bosanski Novi; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Answering the Prosecutor's question, you said that when the war broke out in Croatia, the situation deteriorated and, in your statement, it says that the Muslims refused to be mobilised for the war in Croatia and that then inter-ethnic tensions mounted. Are you referring only to the Muslim population in Bosanski Novi or in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and where did the tensions mount?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, I think in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina but especially in Bosanski Novi. When the Muslims refused to go to fight in Croatia, under instructions --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the end of that reply.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the tensions mounted all over Bosnia and Herzegovina, and especially in Bosanski Novi. I know this because the Muslims refused to be mobilised as reservists of the former JNA or to go to the war front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you answered my question for the first time, did you say that the Muslim population in Bosnia and Herzegovina did that following instructions from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who you are referring to when you say that instructions came from Sarajevo that they should not respond to the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: It was the then-president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who spoke on the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: He spoke on the media, he was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what did he say?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: He said that the Muslims were not duty-bound to be mobilised as reservists and that this was not a Muslim war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm putting these questions to you because they have to do with your description of the situation in Bosanski Novi. You say that that led to a deterioration of the situation. Do you know who it was that declared mobilisation then? And what period of time is this? Can you tell us the month, at least, or the time of year?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it was that declared mobilisation. I think the mobilisation started in 1990, 1991. In 1990 or 1991. And the Muslims, nowadays called Bosniaks, responded to the call-up until the president of the state, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, stated his views on this. And later, the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as an independent state, so they were no longer duty-bound to carry out anybody's instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since your entire testimony has to do with the beginning of the war in Croatia in this year in 1991, and since in your written statement you say, when the war started in Croatia, the Muslims refused to mobilise for the war in Croatia, could you please tell us: Did the mobilisation call apply to all able-bodied males in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina irrespective of ethnic background, and could this have been only an order by the federal authorities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. People got these call-up papers, but when they came to the localities that were noted in the call-up papers, practically all the Bosniaks were sent back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the Muslims refused to be mobilised for the war in Croatia and then the inter-ethnic tensions grew. In what sense were there these tensions in Bosanski Novi, and between whom?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: There were inter-ethnic tensions because Serbs looked down on the Muslims, they had contempt for Muslims, because they did not take part in the war with them. Also in the territory of the entire municipality, the situation was catastrophic. The members of these forces drank excessively and they used their firearms. They would even shoot at places of worship, and even during Muslim funeral services. Quite simply, life in town was unbearable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You're describing now the situation after mobilisation. Are you talking about that or are you talking about the situation when the Muslim population, in response to Alija Izetbegovic's call, refused to mobilise whereas the Serb population responded to the call-up but the war was being waged in the neighbouring Republic of Croatia? Is that the situation you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that at that time, during mobilisation, at check-points there were military reservists and one or two regular policemen. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what kind of check-points were they, who established them, and when?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: These were joint check-points between the members of the armed forces - was it the TO? - and the active police. They were established already in 1991. As a matter of fact, even individuals from SAO Krajina came to the check-points in Bosanski Novi. And who established them, I don't know. It's probably agreement reached between police and military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to understand what period of time this is about, you described the period as the beginning of the war in Croatia, and you say that that is when these check-points existed. Can you at least give us the time of year when this happened in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: 1991, when the Zagreb-Sarajevo railroad was blown up. Reserve and active policemen came from neighbouring municipalities and we guarded the railroads together and we called them joint check-points of civilian and military structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you properly, that these check-points that you're talking about existed in the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi and that they were check-points at which there was duty service on the basis of an agreement reached between civilian and military authorities?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is the way it was precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA represent these military authorities; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, when talking about the police, you said that at that time, the entire reserve force of the police was mobilised and that every village had a police station. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you talked about this problem with mobilisation, the Muslim population refused to mobilise during the call-up and the Serbs did respond to the call-up. Once again I'm asking you to tell us where Bosanski Novi is, in what republic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: In the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the current Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where was it in 1991? Was Bosnia and Herzegovina one of the Yugoslav federal units at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, in 1991, did Croatia, like all other republics, constitute one of the Yugoslav federal units?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, until it declared its independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the occasion of this declaration of independence, did that bring about the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Probably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Bosanski Novi was a town on the very border between the two Yugoslav republics, that is to say Bosnia and Croatia; is that correct, and that the two republics were separated by the bridge?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: The two former republics of Yugoslavia, Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I was referring to 1991. Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you're talking about mobilisation and about the mobilisation of the entire reserve force of the police in Bosanski Novi, and in Bosnia at that time, in 1991, you say in your statement, and you confirmed that today, that there were radio broadcasts and that propaganda was disseminated which only gave rise to an escalation of tensions. Because the question that was put in those broadcasts was, What do you think about Tudjman? And, What do you think about the Ustashas? Did you state that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a morning show called "Instead of Coffee," which was hosted by a journalist from Radio Bosanski Novi --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened at that time in the territory of the neighbouring Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know. There was an armed conflict between the members of the TO of the SAO Krajina, the police, the active JNA, and part of the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago that Croatia was a Yugoslav federal unit, that Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time was a Yugoslav federal unit. This border between Bosnia and Croatia, was there a border crossing there? Was there a police check-point, a border post?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: It was just an administrative border at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You talked about the mounting of tensions in the beginning of the war in Croatia and these problems related to mobilisation, and you described it as follows: That there were reservists in Bosanski Novi every evening, that they were shooting, firing guns into the air, and it was hard to keep them under control. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These reservists that responded to mobilisation, were they soldiers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: These reservists were subordinated according to the chain that existed then to the then-command of the JNA but they were members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At that time when these reservists appeared, is that when the check-points were put up, the ones that you talked about, those that were manned by the army and the police?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These joint check-points, could they carry out their task -- or, first, tell us, what was their task?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Their task was to search vehicles and to check personal identification documents at these check-points and to establish war and peace, but really at that time it was quite impossible. I was at these check-points and I was present when a column of reservists from Loznica was going by. And they fired millions of bullets. They were firing at places of worship; everywhere. It was a state of chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that these mixed police and military check-points could not keep under their control this complicated situation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No, they couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said a few moments ago that the bridge between Dvor Na Uni, which is on one side of the Una, that is in Croatia, in the then-Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, and Bosanski Novi. Now, that bridge is between these two neighbouring republics, and you said that armed groups were crossing this bridge and you said that these were people who were firing rounds of celebratory gun-fire, but you said that they were members of the TO, Martic's Police, and active-duty personnel. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. And one of these policemen killed the late chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you talk about the killing of the late chief, do you mean Mr. Umicevic?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mean him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was the killer of your then-chief caught?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: He was caught the same day and taken to Banja Luka. It was Nikola Krneta.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement -- in your second statement, the second statement you gave to the Prosecutor, you said that you had left work on that day, that you were called up by the duty officer, that you went to the site, and that in that coffee bar you established that the then-Chief Umicevic had been sitting there, that there was shooting and that Nikola Krneta, a military policeman, killed him and that he was then arrested.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened to him after that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did state that. The chief had heard that there was a breakdown in law and order in that coffee bar, and since he lived in the neighbourhood, he was on his way home and he went to see what was going on. He found the owner of the coffee bar there and he sat at a table and talked to him and the Krneta -- the man called Krneta came and he fired a round into the chief's head, and then he -- this man was taken to Banja Luka and I don't know happened. And also the owner of the cafe was arrested too, but the following day I saw that he was released from prison.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask the witness to please speak slower, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I state that Chief Umicevic was a Serb who was chief of police in Bosanski Novi and that in this gun-fire, he was killed by this Krneta who was a military policeman, also a Serb?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talked about that chaos that the police could not keep under control on that day, you talked about armed people who were crossing that bridge, who were coming from the war zones in the neighbouring Croatia. You mentioned Martic's Police. What did this Martic's Police wear, these people that you call the Martic police?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Novi, people knew who members of Martic's Police were. They had camouflage uniforms, white belts. In that police, there were men who had broken the law previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that these people in camouflage uniforms were Martic's Police?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't say on their foreheads that they were Martic's Police, but people knew. Everybody in the police station knew who belonged to Martic's Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this to us, who it was that belonged to this police of Martic's. Who were these people, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: In the context of the police, I am not involving the active-duty civilian policemen. They were very fair. These are people who either in 1990 or 1991, I cannot say exactly, as far as I know, they were trained. They were given special training in Knin. They were trained and educated only to carry out special tasks. Since I know who the members were from the territory of Bosanski Novi, before, they had an inclination towards perpetrating crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you say that these persons who were being trained were persons from the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Novi. Can you tell us who it was that sent them down there for this training in Knin where you claim this happened?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: They were not only from the territory of Bosanski Novi. They came from the territory of all the municipalities of Bosanska Krajina. Most probably these problem -- these people were rallied together through the SDS, because when the SDS came to power, they tried to change the structure of the reserve police force in Bosanski Novi where the people who were not eligible, under quotation marks, were removed and they wanted to have admitted into the police only people who suited them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down, both, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, the interpreters are complaining, both of you are talking very fast. Can you please speak slowly and give each other an opportunity to answer. In other words, when counsel asks a question, will you please stop a little bit and -- for the interpreters to interpret, before you answer. Similarly, you, Mr. Milovancevic, after you've received the answer, stop a little bit for the interpreters to interpret before you ask the next question. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, these people who you called members of Martic's Police, they were people from Bosnian municipalities, they were the population of these Bosnian municipalities, who lived there, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: They among others. I don't know if there were any from the SAO Krajina, but they were from the municipalities of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say they had camouflage uniforms and it didn't say on their foreheads that they were Martic's Policemen. You say that people said they were Martic's Policemen. Is it only on the basis of these rumours that you say that they were Martic's Police?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: We knew these people personally. I knew a lot of them. I remember, for example, Goran Ivanovic or Popovic. I'm 100 per cent certain that he was a member Martic's Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean; that he went there for training and had the uniform you described?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When answering the questions of the Prosecutor about Martic's men who crossed the bridge, Martic's Police, you said they wore camouflage uniforms with white belts and took part in robberies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I said they participated in the robbery of the policemen of the Republic of Croatia who surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that topic. My next question is, in answer to the Prosecutor's questions, you said that apart from robbery and looting, they threw an explosive device onto the home of a journalist and then into the home of a florist, and that both of these victims, so to say, were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I said that they threw explosive device, not into the home but the florist's shop, of a lady, and that -- and also the home of the journalist, and that they also looted a fruit and vegetable warehouse belonging to Ibrahim Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When in your second statement you described these events with the bombings, the throwing of the explosive devices, you said that -- that's on page 3 of your second statement, dated the 19th of July -- that -- it's the second paragraph from the top in B/C/S: "A hand grenade was thrown onto Zarif Safic's house. I was on duty at the time. I went there and saw parts of the device. Three Chetniks in uniform were seen throwing the hand grenade. I don't remember the names of the eye witnesses. This crime was never solved." That's what you said to the OTP. And yet today, answering the questions of the OTP, you say Martic's Policemen through an explosive device onto this house. Which of these is true?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, the word "Chetniks" may have been a slip. They were driving a vehicle by the house and they threw the hand grenade from the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are now testifying under oath. Now you say these were military policemen, that they were seen in a moving vehicle. And answering the question of the Prosecutor, you said they were Martic's Policemen. Do you draw a distinction?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Martic's unit was a special purpose unit. It was subordinated to the command of the army. They carried out --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the end of that question -- that answer, rather. You said "they carried out --" Can you finish that sentence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was Martic's Police, with the description we got on the spot of the vehicle and the persons who had passed by in the vehicle and had thrown that hand grenade. It's very hard. It was very hard at that time to distinguish which police belonged to whom, because they were all then under the command of the then-JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say they were military policemen, that you think they were Martic's Police, that it was very difficult to distinguish men from one another, that you don't remember the eye witnesses, that the crime was never solved, and yet, in answer to the Prosecutor's question, you say these were Martic's Policemen.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: According to the information I received on the spot, there is no doubt that they were members of Martic's Police. However, quite a lot of time has elapsed, so I cannot remember every detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described Martic's Policemen as men who wore camouflage uniforms and white belts. In the second statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, on page 3, in paragraph 5 from the top, you say, correcting your previous statement: "In the 7th paragraph on page 5, I mentioned that special military forces arrived from Banja Luka to disarm these extremists. This special group were the Red Berets from Banja Luka. Zupljanin said it was an elite group and that in cooperation with us they can solve all the problems in the town. However, this unit did nothing. It only made the situation worse." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in the then-JNA, members of the military police wore white belts?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And shoulder straps?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, responding to the Prosecutor's questions, you said there was an attempt to establish a commune of Serb municipalities, which would join up with the Krajina in Croatia, and that this was prevented in Bosanski Novi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in the beginning, authority in Bosanski Novi was exercised in such a way that the SDA and the SDS agreed on everything and the problems emerged later on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the throwing of the two explosive devices into the home and the shop of two Muslims, and you mentioned this was in late 1991 or early 1992, you said in your statement to the Prosecutor that the official town authorities publicly opposed these bombings. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I probably did. Officially, the authorities were very perfidious and got out of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the authorities publicly opposed the bombings, can you tell us what this means? Did they issue a public communique condemning such acts?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they issued such a communique and publicly denounced such acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain, then, what this means, when you say that they officially opposed the bombings? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Officially, the authorities never declared themselves in favour of bombings or destruction of property, but the background is well known; that the SDS was behind it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What you say now, is it the same as what it says in your statement to the Prosecutor, the first one of 1999, that the SDS Crisis Staff organised these bombings?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: However, in the corrections to your statement, you also explained that what you said was only an assumption on your part. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: It's possible I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph of your second statement of the 19th of July 2000, which you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor, you correct yourself and you say: "In paragraph 6 on page 4 I mentioned that the Suha Rebra paramilitary group did a job for the Crisis Staff." You say: "I said that because they all had camouflage uniforms and rifles with long barrels and I assumed that they were working for the Crisis Staff, because when the leader of the group was taken off to prison for a crime, he would be released immediately afterwards." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise but when the Defence counsel refers to the previous statement, maybe the witness should have the statement in front of him so he can confirm that he really said it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If he could also refer to the page on the statement and be given a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The last question I put to you, Witness, referred to the end of the second page and the beginning of the third page of your statement of the 19th of July, 2000. That's the second statement you gave to the OTP, where a paramilitary group called Suha Rebra is mentioned. In this part of your statement, did you say: "I assumed they were working for the Crisis Staff, based on what I've just explained. Of course, I don't know what kind of orders they received, but it was evident that the SDS was behind them." Did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the end of this passage mentioning the Suha Rebra, and that's the statement of the 19th of July, 2000, you say: "I also mentioned that the Serbs killed the commander of this group, Petic, because he was a renegade. He was beyond control. I heard this from someone but I don't remember from whom. He was killed sometime in 1994." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did; and yes, he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, he was killed sometimes in 1994, I don't know, is it what you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend is asking you whether it says in your statement that he was killed in 1994.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Prosecutor in 1999, you mention this paramilitary unit, Suha Rebra, as a group of criminals working for the needs of the SDS, that they wore first civilian clothes and, later on, olive-grey uniforms, and that when the SDS lost control over Petic, he was killed by Serb policemen. Is that what you said to the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In your addendum to your statement you said that these people wore camouflage uniforms, but in your first statement to the OTP, you say they wore olive-grey uniforms, and in the end you said that the people you say were criminals were killed by the Serb police. Then you explained that you assume they were working for the SDS. Is all of this based only on your conclusions and assumptions?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No. Not on assumptions. This group of criminals, the so-called Suha Rebra, whose leader was Miroslav Petic, also known as Titin, initially, like all the other members of the TO for Bosnia-Herzegovina, wore a grey -- olive-grey uniforms, and went as volunteers to the war front in Croatia, where they looted and brought back cattle and other things from Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina. They also got drunk and behaved in a rowdy manner and fired shots in town. During the war, there is information that several hundred civilians in the Bosanski Novi municipality were killed by them. Husein Hotic, an inspector of the MUP in Bosanski Novi, was among those who was killed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the date of his killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know under what circumstances the Serb police killed that man in 1994? Were you there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't there. I only heard that he was killed, and even now, on the bridge, there is a memorial plaque to him, on the bridge over the Una in Bosanski Novi. I was then in Travnik, in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But you know for certain that he was killed by the Serbian police?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, whether it was the active or the Serb police, but he was certainly killed on the bridge in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you mentioned the arrival of Mr. Martic in Bosanski Novi, and you mentioned that this was after what happened in Otoka; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned this Otoka, is that the case when Mr. Martic was kept at some check-point in Otoka and arrested and afterwards released?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's Bosanska Otoka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Abdo Habib worked on Mr. Martic's release, what was he in Bosnia-Herzegovina then?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I think he was either the assistant minister or the deputy minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that he, Mr. Martic, on that occasion when he was released, was brought by car from Otoka to Bosanski Novi. Did you see that or hear that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I heard that he was brought there and, while he was in the late chief's office, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether Mr. Martic had been harmed in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In these proceedings, we heard some statements to the effect that Mr. Martic was brought in a helicopter from Otoka to Bosanski Novi. Are you sure that he came by car from Otoka to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I know that he was taken from the small soccer field in front of the school by helicopter. Now, as far as his coming was concerned, I think that he came by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some restaurant in Bosanski Novi where people who belonged to the leadership of the SDS used to come. You said that the restaurant was owned by a man who came to see Martic when he was released and when he was brought to Bosanski Novi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Martic after that in that restaurant?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Not after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that Mr. Babic, who was Prime Minister of SAO Krajina, came to Bosanski Novi too, that he even walked around there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this was 1991 and that the border between the then Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina -- the Yugoslav Republics of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia was an administrative border and that there was free passage.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you believe that it is strange or unnatural if someone crosses a bridge one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I think that's only natural, but this happened when the war in Croatia started, but Croatia was already an independent state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you say the war started in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: 1991. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear when Croatia was recognised as an independent state?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I heard when it was recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: But when was it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. It was 1990 or 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a policeman, you say that Croatia is independent and that it's no longer part of Yugoslavia. On the basis of what knowledge do you state that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, it proclaimed independence and was recognised by the United Nations. It became, therefore, an independent state, like Bosnia-Herzegovina did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that it was admitted into the United Nations in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that but I know that the parliament of the Republic of Croatia declared independence before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ante Markovic was at that time in 1991?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I know very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Honourable Judges who the man was?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: The Prime Minister of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the request of the Federal Executive Council, that is to say the government of Yugoslavia that was headed by this Ante Markovic, the constitutional court of Yugoslavia on the 16th of August, 1991, passed a decision on annulling as anti-constitutional all the decisions of Slovenia and Croatia on secession? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you describe this situation concerning the restaurant, you say that you often came to that restaurant, that you were in front of it, rather, and that you saw that the door was locked and then you wrote down the registration plate numbers of the cars. Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that you saw that some JNA officer came to that restaurant who was commander of the garrison in Cerkezovac and that he would stay until the end of the opening hours of the restaurant; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were several officers and politicians, but I personally knew Kosta Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the parties in Bosanski Novi had their own headquarters, did the SDS have its own headquarters, did the SDA have its own headquarters and these other parties?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: They had their offices, but politicians would meet in that restaurant, and when politicians and military officers met in that restaurant, then the door would be locked and other people did not have access.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So can you know the reason why the restaurant was locked when somebody was sitting in it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the reason would be for it to be locked. A restaurant is a public place where anybody has access. However, in those times, when members of the former JNA would meet, officers, and the top people of the SDS, the door would be locked so they were obviously having some meetings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the restaurant was locked and probably they had some meetings there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever enter after somebody had unlocked the door for you, and did you see any of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I could not enter, nor could anyone else who had not been invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a policeman, did you perhaps have the premises bugged and did you perhaps hear what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: How can you bug a restaurant? We were not in a position to do that. We could not have done that, because it is very well known what kind of policy was waged by the centre of public security in Banja Luka, headed by Zupljanin and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that, Witness. You told us just now that you did not see who it was that was at the restaurant, that you did not hear what people were saying. You said that you saw that when the restaurant would close, people would leave the restaurant. Can you tell us, what is this end of opening hours?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: The end of opening hours is the time when a restaurant is closed. However, at that time not everyone had access to the restaurant. A restaurant should be a public place, that everybody has access to. However, if a certain group of people are sitting there, locked up in there, the question is: What are they doing there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that you are describing alleged meetings of the leadership of the SDS and the top military people in that restaurant without knowing who it was that attended them, without knowing what they talked about, and because the door was locked in a restaurant that is privately owned and that the owner can lock and close any time, you are inferring that it's some kind of conspiracy; is that right, Witness?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, an owner cannot lock the door to his restaurant and say somebody can come in and somebody cannot come in, and thus choose his guests. However, when the restaurant is closed without the presence of other citizens, there is absolutely grounds for suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you are a citizen of Muslim faith; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you following the leadership of the Muslim party, the SDA, then? Did you see where they were meeting, whether they were locking doors, and were you a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of the SDA, and we equally followed both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said to us a moment ago that you heard that Alija Izetbegovic, as leader of the SDA, called on -- upon the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina not to respond to call-up, to mobilisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, parallel to the war in Croatia, anything happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina in terms of arming the population on ethnic grounds?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I know what I could see, and what I saw on television. In Bosanski Novi, I know how a certain number of individuals of Muslim ethnicity were armed. They bought weapons from members of the former JNA or reservists who sold these weapons to them. When the special unit of the Red Berets came, they went from house to house, and judging by the already-recorded registration numbers of these weapons, they asked for these weapons to be handed back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that some bought weapons in a premeditated fashion and others then collected it back in premeditated fashion?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Some got them free of charge and others bought weapons, but what they bought they had to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the report of the Ministry of the Interior of the Yugoslav Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from mid-June 1991? It's a daily security bulletin, dated the 26th of June 1991, which speaks about great anxiety among people in Bosanski Novi, Bosanska Dubica, Bosanska Krupa, and Velika Kladusa because of the concentration of big forces of the Croatian MUP in the area. Do you know of this information? Was this kind of information sent to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't heard of it and I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this daily security bulletin of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the end of June 1991 says that this exceptional anxiety among citizens in Bosanski Novi leads to the self-organisation of citizens, to the setting up of night guards and the blockade of roads and that it leads to requests made by citizens of all ethnic backgrounds to receive weapons. Have you heard of such a report?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No. I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that citizens in Dvor Na Uni, at the bridge between Dvor Na Uni and Bosanski Novi, that is to say on the bridge at the outskirts of your own town, put up a blockade on the bridge, that the citizens themselves did that in June 1991?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I know that there were some problems there and in Matijevici also. That is a village when you get out of Bosanski Novi. They were putting flags there and different emblems, but what actually happened there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that armed people who came from the territory of the neighbouring Republic of Croatia where there was a war, regardless of whether they were soldiers of the JNA or reservists or, as you call them, Martic's men, that they came to Bosanski Novi. But do you know anything about transporting women and children from Hrvatska Dubica and Hrvatska Kostajnica to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the transport of Serb people from Croatia to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were these women and children?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Oh, there were women and children there and also men who were employed. They simply left their employment, from the territory of the entire Republic of Croatia, and then they went to Bosanski Novi, of course, if they originated from Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that my colleague has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I just wanted to know the period of time you are referring to about these women and children coming to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, my last two questions had to do with June 1991. As for my last question, I asked you whether you heard, and you said yes, that women and children from Croatia crossed over to the territory of Bosanski Novi. Can you tell us what their ethnic background was of these people who came to Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Serbs for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us how they came; on foot, by car, on tractors, buses, in an organised or unorganised way?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of any organised convoys. People came as they could. Mostly on different vehicles. At that time, there were still trains that were operating, so some people came on train too, and on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people this involved?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly but I know that there was a mass of people who were born in Bosanski Novi and who had relatives there and who worked in Sisak, Zagreb, and so on and so forth, and they came to see their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that these were masses of people. And you told us that these were not people from the other side of the Una River, which was between Dvor Na Uni and Bosanski Novi, but that these were ethnic Serbs from Zagreb, Sisak, faraway towns in Croatia. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Yes, from all over Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So why was it that they came to your town; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Well, probably to avoid a war, just like I left Bosanski Novi eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of things did these people bring along? Did you check that at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they were bringing along. I was at the check-point only once or twice. I was the head of sector for the entire town of Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were head of sector, and since you worked in the police at the time, can you tell us what that word means, that there were many people, ethnic Serbs, who came from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. What can you say, how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but since I went to the neighbouring areas that gravitated towards the municipality of Bosanski Novi, and to the villages too, I came across people who I knew earlier on, and they told me that they had left their apartments, their houses, et cetera, and that they had come to stay with relatives and others. I cannot exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please slow down. I can hear that the interpreter is struggling to keep pace. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there were many people and you don't know the exact number, was it tens or hundreds or thousands? Can you tell us what the order of magnitude was?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA KRUPIC
utterances.text: Hundreds, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have just completed a particular topic so perhaps it would be right to take the break now, to adjourn for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. We are adjourned until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning. If you can please be back here, Mr. Krupic. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of March 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
